issues.legal_issue: The urban vacant-land ceiling legislation advances the constitutional objectives of distributing material resources for the common good and preventing concentration of wealth.
material_facts: The legislation imposed ceilings on vacant land in urban agglomerations and provided for acquisition of land held in excess of those ceilings.
The legislation’s stated objects included preventing concentration, speculation and profiteering in urban land and achieving equitable distribution for the common good.
The legislation was included in the Ninth Schedule and was challenged as inconsistent with the relevant Directive Principles.
issues.conclusion: The legislation is constitutionally valid as a whole, except for the specified transfer restriction invalidated under section 27(1); defects in individual provisions do not establish that the legislation as a whole fails to advance the constitutional objectives.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 39(b) and 39(c) address equitable distribution of material resources for the common good and prevention of concentration of wealth. The Court applied the protection of Article 31-C as it stood before the Forty-second Amendment and considered the Ninth Schedule framework in light of Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala and Waman Rao v. Union of India.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_urban_land_c: A proceeding challenges the constitutionality of legislation imposing ceilings on urban vacant land.
predicates.law_limits_urban_vacant_land_holdings: The challenged law restricts the amount of vacant urban land a person may hold.
predicates.scheme_provides_for_acquisition_and_comm: The law provides for taking excess land and distributing or using it for the common good.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a law that limits urban vacant land holdings and provides for acquisition and common-good distribution, the rule treats the legislation as valid except for any separately invalid provision.

issues.legal_issue: Defining a ceiling unit as an individual, that person’s spouse, and their unmarried minor children does not violate equality merely because it excludes major children or joint-family arrangements.
material_facts: The law defined a family by reference to an individual, that individual’s spouse, and their unmarried minor children.
The petitioners argued that the definition treated families with minor children differently from households with adult children or joint-family arrangements when applying the land ceiling.
The Court concluded that the definition did not inevitably cause concentration of wealth and accorded with contemporary urban living conditions.
issues.conclusion: The statutory definition of family is not arbitrary or violative of Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not invalidate a legislative classification merely because it draws distinctions among family arrangements; the Court considered whether the definition was arbitrary and whether it necessarily produced the alleged concentration of wealth. Krishna Iyer, J. considered the definition consistent with current urban family conditions.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_urban_land_c: A proceeding challenges the constitutionality of legislation imposing ceilings on urban vacant land.
predicates.ceiling_unit_includes_individual_spouse_: The law calculates the relevant household unit by including an individual, the spouse, and their unmarried minor children.
predicates.definition_does_not_inevitably_concentra: The definition does not necessarily or inevitably permit concentration of land in a few hands.

issues.definition: When a ceiling-law challenge concerns a household unit comprising an individual, spouse, and unmarried minor children, and that definition does not inevitably concentrate land, the rule treats the definition as consistent with equality.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory maximum on the amount payable for acquired excess vacant land is not unconstitutional when the amount is not illusory or confiscatory.
material_facts: The law prescribed principles for calculating the amount payable when excess vacant land was acquired and imposed a maximum amount payable in any case.
The petitioners argued that the maximum was arbitrary and illusory because it did not vary with the full extent or market value of the land acquired.
The Court held that the maximum amount was not merely nominal or confiscatory.
issues.conclusion: The maximum amount payable is valid and does not violate Articles 14 or 31(2).
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as amended by the Twenty-fifth Amendment, made the adequacy of the amount payable non-justiciable; the Court nevertheless considered whether the amount was illusory. The Court relied on the approach to Article 31(2) in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, R.C. Cooper v. Union of India, State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing Co. Ltd., and State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compulsory_a: A proceeding challenges the constitutionality of the amount payable for compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.law_sets_payment_principles_and_a_maximu: The law specifies a method or principles for calculating payment and also sets a maximum payable amount.
predicates.maximum_amount_is_not_merely_nominal: The amount payable under the maximum is not merely nominal or illusory.

issues.definition: When an acquisition-payment challenge concerns a law that sets payment principles and a maximum that is not merely nominal, the rule treats the maximum as constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory power to dispose of acquired excess vacant land is valid when its exercise is governed by the requirement that disposal subserve the common good.
material_facts: The law authorized allotment of acquired excess vacant land for purposes connected with industry and other stated purposes, and defined industry broadly.
The law also directed that acquired vacant land be disposed of to subserve the common good.
The Court treated the common-good direction as governing disposal and held that an allotment that does not serve that purpose may be struck down.
issues.conclusion: Section 23 is valid, but each disposal of excess vacant land must subserve the common good; a disposal that does not do so is liable to be struck down.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 39(b) and 39(c) inform the common-good purpose of the legislation. The Court read the broad allotment power consistently with the common-good direction and the Act’s purpose, applying the principle that statutory language may be read down to sustain a law while preserving judicial review of excess or mala fide exercises of power.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_excess_land_: A proceeding challenges the legal validity of a scheme for disposing of land acquired in excess of an urban holding limit.
predicates.acquired_land_is_disposed_of_under_a_com: The governing scheme requires acquired land to be disposed of in a manner serving the common good.

issues.definition: When a challenged excess-land disposal scheme requires disposal for the common good, the rule permits a disposal only if it serves that good.

issues.legal_issue: A restriction requiring prior permission to transfer built-up urban property within the permitted ceiling area is invalid to that extent.
material_facts: The law required prior permission for specified transfers of urban or urbanisable land with a building, or part of a building.
The restriction applied to property within the ceiling area that its holder was permitted to retain.
The Act imposed its ceiling on vacant land and left built-up property outside that ceiling scheme.
issues.conclusion: Section 27(1) is invalid insofar as it restricts transfer of urban or urbanisable land with a building, or part of a building, within the ceiling area.
issues.legal_principle: A transfer restriction on built-up property within the permitted ceiling area falls outside the scope of a law directed to ceilings on vacant urban land and is invalid to that extent. The Court relied on the right to dispose of property under Article 19(1)(f), as then in force, and the reasoning in Excel Wear v. Union of India.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_tra: A proceeding challenges a statutory restriction on transferring property.
predicates.property_includes_a_building_or_part_of_: The property subject to the restriction includes a building or a portion of a building.
predicates.property_is_within_the_permitted_ceiling: The property falls within the amount of land its holder is permitted to retain.

issues.definition: When a transfer-restriction challenge concerns property that includes a building or part of one and falls within the permitted ceiling, the rule invalidates the restriction for that property.
